chapter: Bebop New York and the early breaks
title: Practicing time with Oscar Peterson records and Don Byas's Cherokee
summary: He has students practice with Oscar Peterson records without drums, and recalls practicing a Don Byas Cherokee four-beat so Bud Powell's tempo felt easy.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I’m talking about actual time. So I get all my students, they have to go out and buy one or two Oscar Peterson duo or trio records with no drums. The time of course they don’t need it, the time is sensational, and they have to practice with that as part of the lesson — to © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -6-

get a groove. But a lot of people don’t practice rhythm. But when I was young, for some reason, I don’t want to sound like oh wasn’t I so smart, it seemed like common sense — gee if I’m going to go to New York and try to sit in, you know, what if Bud Powell called “Cherokee” and it happened. And I had a record of “Cherokee” by Don Byas that was faster than anything in the world. It went like this in two beat [sings]. And the drummer played it a two beat style — do you follow what I mean?

I played it four beat. I went [scats], and I would do that three or four times a day. So when Bud Powell played his “Cherokee” it wasn’t as fast as Don Byas’ “Cherokee.” I felt like I was on cruising speed, yeah.
